speaker_notes: The preacher is 'Pat' — the worship leader prays at 0:38:07 'that you would anoint Pat to bring the message of purity to our hearts', and at 1:02:05 he calls his own rendering of 1 Thess 4:4 'the pastor Pat paraphrase'. Heavy autobiography identifies him further: wife Cindy (married 45 years, three kids, four grandkids), son Matthew born ~Dec 1981, daughter Caitlyn who turned 16 in 2006; he was a youth pastor who did Dallas Theological Seminary's Masters of Biblical Studies over two summers in the mid-1980s. Local Tucson cues: Bear Canyon Library, 'Tankerie [Tanque Verde] to Wentworth', Park Place Mall, Center for Arizona Policy voter guides, Fellowship Bible Church. Audience is a full intergenerational service ('the whole assembly of ages'), and he repeatedly frames the message as training for parents and grandparents ('I'm creating a NGC, next generation equipping course'). He explicitly says this continues last week's message on pleasing God ('here we are back to this big picture that we started last week').
boundary_note: The worship leader's prayer ends at 0:38:26 ('the church said, Amen'). Pat begins speaking at 0:38:28 ('It's so exciting to be here and worshiping the Lord'), moves into his framing remarks about talking about sex, prays at 0:39:15, reads 1 Thessalonians 4:1-8 at 0:39:52-0:41:01, and preaches. He closes reading 1 Thess 4:9-10 at 1:15:39 and prays from 1:16:55, ending 'Amen' at 1:18:03; the band's 'Speak, O Lord' starts at 1:18:22. Announcements before (0:12:21-0:17:20) and the second closing prayer plus 'let's do lunch' announcement after 1:27:10 are excluded.

attribution.notes: Alistair Begg and Truth For Life are never named, and the sermon is never presented as anyone else's outline. The named sources are exactly the ones Begg also names in these two sermons, and in two cases they are the very quotations Begg uses. At 1:03:57: 'CS Lewis had the best expression on this. He says, "If you really want to know what the intentions of a guy are and you're going to have sex, find out what they do five minutes after the act is over." And then he says, "After the cigarettes are all smoked, rarely does one keep the rapper."' — Begg (Part Two): 'C.S. Lewis puts it as graphically as any. When he says if you want to know how much interest a man has ... watch him five minutes afterwards and then he says no one keeps the packet when they've smoked the cigarettes.' At 1:13:58: 'what I love about this is JB Phillips ... he paraphrases it and he makes clear one word' — Begg: 'Philips paraphrases it, make a clean cut with all sexual immorality.' Two borrowed items are stripped of their attribution entirely: Begg quotes the commentator I. H. Marshall by name — 'Marshall puts it in this way where things are evil, the Christian attitude is necessarily one of abstention and not of moderation' — and at 1:15:13 the FBC preacher delivers it as his own summary: 'when things are evil, the Christian attitude is not to be one of moderation, but it's to be abstinence.' Likewise Begg's 'it's said by some' framing survives at 0:53:40 ('It's said by some that the conditions in which Paul lived in century 1 are very different from our own') without any hint that the answering argument is also borrowed. The one genuinely signposted source is his own: 'In 1982, Cindy and I were at a conference ... marriage counselor Norm Wright posed a question' (0:41:01).

outline_comparison: Partly the same skeleton, and the shared part is the expository spine. The FBC sermon opens and closes with material that is entirely its own (Norm Wright, the seminary-summer story, the Honda Accord, Babylon/public schools), but the moment it turns to the text at 0:46:54 it follows Begg's Part One almost step for step: the same three proof texts in the same order (John 8, 2 Cor 5, Eph 5:10), the same thesis sentence about aspirations and the praise of his glory, the same 'do we have the right to be so bold and forceful' objection, the same Corinth/Aphrodite/Thessalonica background answering the same rhetorical question, the same reading of vv.3-8 as an imaginary dialogue with the same sequence of objections, the same 3:13→5:23 encouragement with the same '11 years / no girlfriend' teenager, and the same closing run of sanctification-by-scripture → marriage list → Phillips 'clean cut' → mangled creature → tonsils → abstinence not moderation. Part Two is used far less but is not untouched: the C.S. Lewis cigarette quote, the poison-in-beautiful-wrapping image, the single/divorced/widowed question and the Pharisee warning all come from it. What FBC adds is not a different structure but interpolated personal illustration inside Begg's frame, plus one genuinely independent device (the bird's-eye view/valley picture) carried over from his own previous week.

original_material.summary: Roughly half the sermon by clock time is the FBC preacher's own, and it is genuinely his: two long autobiographical narratives, a controlling visual metaphor he brought from his own previous week, a distinctive pedagogical frame (equipping parents and grandparents to have this conversation), and a set of blunt local applications about dating that have no counterpart in Begg. He is also a different kind of preacher — anecdotal, Americanised, politically engaged — where Begg is expository and doctrinal. What he does not supply is the exposition: every time he leaves a story and returns to the text, he returns to Begg's sequence, Begg's illustrations and often Begg's sentences. Notably absent from the FBC version are Begg's crisis-process-crisis doctrine of sanctification, the drill sergeant illustration, Elisabeth Elliot's '60 seconds a minute', the Romans 5/6/8 chain, John Stott's two statements and his testimony on singleness, and the Romans 1 material — so the borrowing is selective, not a wholesale reading of the manuscript.

personalisation_patterns: Begg's neutral 'the individual' in the imaginary dialogue becomes a named character with a folksy label — 'the earth child' talking to heaven-bound Paul — which makes an adopted device look like an invented one.

Begg's 'I've been helped by viewing this paragraph here as one half of a conversation' becomes 'Imagine yourself as the teacher of a conversation ... you'll start seeing vision for your life and your ministry': the reader's aid Begg offers is re-pitched as the audience's own ministry tool.

Borrowed illustrations are introduced with markers of personal disclosure: the marriage-list illustration arrives as 'I think you'll get it. And I'll share this' (1:12:46), and Marshall's sentence arrives as 'So, let's put it this way' (1:15:13).

British details are Americanised inside otherwise verbatim borrowings: 'cinema' becomes 'movie' (and gains 'you text'); Begg's 'wee bit over the top' becomes 'reading it over the top'; Begg's 'man' in 1 Thess 4:8 becomes the NIV's 'a human being'.

Attribution is unevenly preserved: J.B. Phillips and C.S. Lewis (whom Begg names) are named; I. H. Marshall (whom Begg also names) is dropped and his sentence absorbed; Begg himself is never named at any point.

Begg's background material is compressed and then topped with a local joke — the Aphrodite/Corinth paragraph is reproduced closely and then capped with 'a lot like Vegas ... what happens in Corenth stays in Corenth'.

Where Begg gives a doctrinal excursus (crisis-process-crisis, Romans 5-8, the drill sergeant), FBC substitutes a family anecdote of comparable length (the Honda Accord), so the borrowed spine is padded out with original narrative rather than original exegesis.
Traces of reading rather than handling the text: 'verse five of chapter 23' for 1 Thess 5:23, and 'Proverbs 19:9' for Psalm 119:9 — both points where Begg's spoken source gives no clean citation.
rating_rationale: This sermon is not more independent than the others in the series once you look past the personal material — the machine's 6.5% coverage badly understates it, because most of the reuse is compressed paraphrase rather than verbatim strings. Every element of the exposition is Begg's: the opening trio of proof texts in his order, his thesis sentence about aspirations and the praise of his glory reproduced word for word, his 'bold and forceful' objection, his Corinth/Aphrodite background answering his rhetorical question, his imaginary dialogue as the sermon's entire organising device with its objections in his sequence, his 3:13→5:23 encouragement, his eleven-years teenager, his marriage-list illustration, his Phillips 'clean cut', his roadkill and his tonsils, and Marshall's line with the attribution removed. Part Two is used less but is demonstrably in hand: the C.S. Lewis cigarette quote with its superlative framing, the poison-in-beautiful-wrapping image, the single/divorced/widowed question and the closing Pharisee warning. What holds the rating at 7 rather than higher is that roughly half the running time is authentically the preacher's own — the Norm Wright frame, the near-miss on the flight to Dallas, the bird's-eye-view metaphor from his own previous week, the Honda Accord, the dating counsel — and that he leaves out large tracts of Begg (the crisis-process-crisis doctrine, the drill sergeant, Elisabeth Elliot, Stott, Romans 1). The result is a genuinely personal sermon built on a borrowed and unacknowledged expository skeleton.

caveats: The FBC text is YouTube auto-captions and the Begg text is Whisper ASR; both mangle words ('conmening' for condemning, 'widowerower', 'Tankerie' for Tanque Verde, 'rapper' for wrapper, 'Corenth', 'JB Phillips he paradise he paraphrases'; Begg's 'Elizabeth Elliott', 'indesolable', 'Samist' for psalmist). Exact wording should be checked against audio before publication, though the overlaps here are far too long and too specific to be transcription artefacts.

Both men are preaching 1 Thessalonians 4:1-8 from the NIV, so shared Scripture wording is expected and proves nothing. Alignment Regions 1, 2, 8 and 10 are essentially the biblical text and are excluded from the case; Regions 7, 11, 12 and 13 are the biblical text wrapped in Begg's own connective phrasing, and only the wrapper counts as evidence.

Some shared items are genuinely common property in conservative evangelical preaching and are treated as weak evidence: the Corinth/Aphrodite background (standard commentary material, though the wording here is not), warnings about the Pharisee spirit, 'we don't break God's laws, God's laws break us', and the general claim that the first century was as immoral as our own.

The C.S. Lewis and J.B. Phillips quotations circulate widely and could in principle have been picked up elsewhere; what makes them evidential is that they appear alongside Begg's framing language, in Begg's order, inside passages that are otherwise near-verbatim.

The alignment tool's scripture guesses are unreliable for this file — it labelled the marriage-list illustration 'possible_scripture Exodus 16' and Begg's thesis sentence 'likely_scripture Ephesians 1'. Region classifications above are my own reading of the texts, not the tool's.

The machine pairing reported 6.5% coverage for Part One and 1.8% for Part Two. Both figures materially understate the dependence: the largest borrowing (the imaginary-dialogue structure that organises roughly twenty minutes of the sermon) is a structural reuse that token-overlap scoring cannot see, and much of the rest is close paraphrase that falls below the identity threshold.

Grep across all 22 Begg transcripts in source_transcripts/ found the distinctive phrases ('aspirations ... praise of his glory', 'prominent notions', 'ethical Christian behavior', tonsils, 'concrete example') only in these two sermons, so there is no sign of a third Begg sermon being drawn on here. The preacher does say he began this 'big picture' last week, which corresponds to Begg's volume2/01-pleasinggod — a separate sermon that should be checked in its own review.
